lesson_title: One Bale of Cotton, Three Continents
hook_text: A single bale of cotton in a Manchester mill in 1820 connects Africa, America and Britain, and it leads all the way to Kimberley.
clip_script: Follow one bale of cotton. It was grown in the American South by enslaved people of African descent, whose ancestors were carried across the Atlantic on the Middle Passage. It crossed the ocean to Liverpool, a city grown rich on the slave trade. In Manchester, a steam engine burning British coal drove machines that spun and wove it faster than a hundred pairs of hands. That is the Industrial Revolution: machines, steam, coal and factories, starting in Britain around 1750. Historians still argue about how much the slave trade paid for it. Most agree it was one important piece among several. But factories are hungry. They need raw materials, customers and minerals. In 1860 workers from India arrived to cut sugar cane in Natal. In 1867 diamonds were found near the Orange River. In 1886, gold. The hungry factories had reached southern Africa.
visual_style: A whiteboard map of the Atlantic with a cotton bale travelling a triangle of arrows, then a steam engine in a mill, then a line stretching south to Natal, Kimberley and the Witwatersrand with the dates appearing.
pacing: A steady journey along the route, a pause on the debate, then three quick dates.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and see how the Industrial Revolution reached South Africa.
